clue.text: Attend tailor, me? Unlikely

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement of the three words signals that their letters are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A scruffy speaker scoffs at the idea of ever visiting a tailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlikely' rearranges ATTEND TAILOR ME, and the whole clue is also the definition: a ragged person is the last one who would go to a tailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragamuffin in torn clothes is just the sort of person who would never visit a tailor, so the whole clue describes one.

clue.text: Spooner's embarrassing honest folk in play

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the phrase meant by the clue has its initial sounds exchanged

parts.note: embarrassing someone is shaming them
the true are honest, faithful people

explanation.surface: A drama in which upright people are humiliated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Embarrassing honest folk' is 'the shaming of the true'; swap the SH and T sounds to get the Shakespeare comedy. The answer runs on into 23 Down.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Shakespeare's comedy about Petruchio and Katherina, so it is a play.

clue.text: Examples of "stating the bleeding obvious" suit Mrs Faulty

indicators.note: something faulty is out of order, so these letters must be put into a new order; also a pun on Fawlty

explanation.surface: Sybil Fawlty is said to be a source of remarks that state the bleeding obvious, a phrase from Fawlty Towers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs Faulty' recalls Sybil, wife of Basil Fawlty in the British sitcom Fawlty Towers, whose 'specialist subject' was 'the bleeding obvious'; 'Faulty' rearranges SUIT MRS.
explanation.definitionFit: Truisms are self-evident statements that everyone already accepts, exactly what stating the obvious produces.

clue.text: Models are not liable to have bottom wiped by Swedish bloke

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom is the last letter, so the final letter is removed

parts.note: someone not liable for a tax or duty is exempt
Lars is a common Swedish man's name

explanation.surface: Fashion models, freed of liability, get a nappy change from a Swede.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have bottom wiped' drops the last letter of EXEMPT, the bottom one in a down answer, leaving EXEMP.
explanation.definitionFit: Exemplars are perfect examples to copy, which is what models are in the sense of patterns.

clue.text: Ward problem

parts.note: the word ward is draw written backwards, so the answer read as an instruction ('draw' turned round) produces it

explanation.surface: A hospital ward has some trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer, read as wordplay, says to write DRAW the other way round, which gives the clue word 'Ward'.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawback is a disadvantage or snag, which is one sense of a problem.

clue.text: Framework said to follow April Fools?

indicators.note: said signals that the phrase is to be heard rather than written, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: April Fools' Day pranks would be followed, a month later, by May tricks

explanation.surface: A structure supposedly comes after the pranks of April Fools' Day.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsy: tricks that follow April's would be May tricks, which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A matrix is a surrounding structure or setting in which something develops, so it is a framework.

clue.text: Sign up to take part in bar billiards

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top
the answer takes only part of the words that follow, so it is concealed in them

explanation.surface: Sign up for a game of bar billiards, a British pub table game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take part in' points to ARBIL inside 'bar billiards'; 'up' turns it round to give the star sign. Bar billiards is a pub table game.
explanation.definitionFit: Libra, the scales, is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

clue.text: Mansion built for personal pleasure

indicators.note: a building is put together, so the letters are assembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A grand house was constructed just for its owner's enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Built' rearranges MANSION.
explanation.definitionFit: Onanism is masturbation, a euphemistic kind of pleasure one gives oneself.

clue.text: Solver's old half-length cycle round ambassador

parts.note: the solver is addressed as you, so solver's means your
ex means former, so it stands for old

indicators.note: turning the letters round signals that they are rearranged
half of the hyphenated word keeps just its first three letters

explanation.surface: A bike ride of half the usual length goes around an envoy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-length' looks like a description of the cycle ride, but 'half' works on 'length' alone; 'round' then shuffles that with CYCLE.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the formal form of address used to an ambassador, so it can stand for one.

clue.text: In high spirits once over German worker

parts.note: ex means formerly, as once does
über is the German word for over
the ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: Someone was once cheerful about a German labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over German' means the German word for over, über. Ants are the usual crossword workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Exuberant means full of energy and excitement, being in high spirits.

clue.text: Prime cuts of beef — rare and, very occasionally, well done

indicators.note: the prime cuts are the leading pieces, the first letter cut from each following word

explanation.surface: A cookery note on prime beef, served rare, and only seldom well done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well done' looks like the steak's cooking but is the cheer of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravo is an exclamation of applause, the same as saying well done to someone.

clue.text: To whom the mouse and the lion pose a problem

definitions.text: To whom the mouse and the lion

indicators.note: a problem is something to be worked out, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A mouse and a lion set somebody a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'to whom we owe the fable of the mouse and the lion'. 'Problem' rearranges POSE A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lion and the Mouse is one of the fables credited to the ancient Greek storyteller.

clue.text: In wrong gear? That's right, officer

indicators.note: in places the word for gear inside the word for wrong

parts.note: bad means wrong, as in bad behaviour
rig is gear or equipment
ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: Someone in the wrong kit is told it's correct by an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' stands for 'that is', i.e. IE.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigadier is an army officer ranking above a colonel.

clue.text: A case of home position

parts.note: being in means being at home
a stance is a position or posture

explanation.surface: A legal matter about where someone stands at home.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is an example or occurrence, as is a case in the phrase 'in this case'.

clue.text: Brief ascent with short cut to reach the top

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a climb is an ascent

indicators.note: short again means the final letter is lost

parts.note: to axe is to cut

explanation.surface: A quick climb via a shortcut to get to the summit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' trims CLIMB to CLIM and 'short' trims AXE to AX.
explanation.definitionFit: A climax is the highest point or culmination, which the top of something represents.

clue.text: Look up fish at university in France, a mythical creature

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look
taken as written
the gar is a long-snouted fish
OU is the Open University, Britain's distance-learning university

explanation.surface: Someone checks on a fish at a French college and finds a monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look up' seems one phrase but splits in two. The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university; 'in France' places the creature in French folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: The loup-garou is the werewolf of French folklore, a legendary beast.

clue.text: Hard rain's gonna fall for 23

indicators.note: letters that fall come down in a jumble, signalling a rearrangement

parts.note: the 's here means is, so only the word rain gives letters

explanation.surface: Bob Dylan's song 'A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall', pointed at a scold.
explanation.walkthrough: '23' refers to the answer to 23 Down, a scolding woman. 'Gonna fall' rearranges HARD RAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A harridan is a bad-tempered, nagging old woman, much as a shrew is.

clue.text: Tawdry trim with no end of ostentation

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so the letter that follows is taken out

parts.note: to garnish is to trim or decorate food

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Cheap-looking decoration without a trace of showiness, a paradox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of ostentation' is N; 'with no' takes it out of GARNISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Garish means showy and cheaply bright, the same as tawdry.

clue.text: Morning caller's rest, woolly jumper on top

indicators.note: in a down clue, on top puts the jumper's word above the rest

parts.note: a roo, a kangaroo, is a jumper

indicators.note: woolly means fuzzy or muddled, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A cockerel is resting with a woolly sweater on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like a British sweater, encouraged by 'woolly'; it is a kangaroo. 'Woolly' rearranges REST to STER.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster crows at dawn, so it calls out each morning.

clue.text: Spread (eg butter) endlessly round a loaf of bread

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters go around the letter that follows
spread signals the letters are scattered into a new order
endlessly removes the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Spread butter, for example, round a loaf of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket reads as a cooking aside, but its words are the fodder; the shuffled result BGUETTE goes 'round' A.
explanation.definitionFit: A baguette is a long thin French loaf.

clue.text: What's warm?

parts.note: the answer read as wordplay says to rearrange the word thaw, and doing so produces this word

explanation.surface: A simple question: what is warm?
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: treat 'out' as an anagram signal on THAW and the result is WHAT, the clue's first word.
explanation.definitionFit: To thaw out is to warm up something frozen until it softens.

clue.text: Advanced knot securing loose end

indicators.note: securing means holding, so the knot's word goes around the letter

parts.note: a hitch is a kind of knot

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A sophisticated knot ties off a loose end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose end' is E, the last letter of 'loose', held inside HITCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Hi-tech describes advanced, sophisticated technology.

clue.text: Rank by comparison of writer's novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: the 's here gives its S, so the full fodder is OF WRITERS

explanation.surface: Rating an author's novel against others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like a verb or a position but means foul-smelling; 'novel' rearranges OF WRITERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Frowsty means stale and musty, so its comparative is a smellier, ranker condition.

clue.text: See 1
Aim when holy and delicate for a key change

indicators.note: changing musical key from F to G means swapping those letters

parts.note: frail means delicate

explanation.surface: A musician's aim, sacred yet fragile, demands a modulation.
explanation.walkthrough: F and G are musical keys, so 'a key change' swaps F for G in FRAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A grail is an object of quest, and the Holy Grail is the proverbial ultimate goal.

clue.text: No lover has a broken heart

indicators.note: broken means smashed into pieces, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A jilted person nursing heartbreak swears off love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges HEART.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who hates is the opposite of someone who loves.

clue.text: Covering party in spilt red wine

indicators.note: in puts the party's word inside the jumbled letters
spilt wine splashes everywhere, so the letters are scattered

parts.note: a do is a party

explanation.surface: A duvet at a party gets red wine spilt on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spilt' makes EIDERWN, which the party word goes 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eiderdown is a quilt, a bed covering filled with down.

clue.text: Business that's promising to lose weight with sturdy exercise

parts.note: losing weight is to grow thin

indicators.note: exercise puts the letters through their paces into a new order

explanation.surface: A fitness firm promises weight loss through tough workouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To lose weight' gives GROW THIN; 'exercise' rearranges STURDY into DUSTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A sector expanding fast holds promise for investors and commerce.
